title: How your phone knows the distance (it only measures speed) 📍 #shorts #shortsfeed #math #maths
description:
Your phone and your car only ever measure one thing directly: your SPEED, moment to
moment. So how do they know the DISTANCE you traveled?

They add it up. In any tiny slice of time, distance ≈ speed × time. Add up all those
slivers and you get the AREA under the speed–time graph — that's an integral:

   distance = ∫ v dt

Watch a short trip — speed up to 20 m/s, cruise, then brake. The area under the curve
fills in as you go, and it lands on exactly 140 meters (30 + 80 + 30). That area IS
the distance. It's the same math behind your car's trip meter, your running app, and
GPS.

No narration — watch the area become the distance. More "math in the real world"
coming.

title: INTRODUCTION TO CALCULUS for dummies
The Most Satisfying Calculus Trick You'll See Today! 🧠 | Smooth Integrals
description:
Can you solve this beautiful integration problem? At first glance, mixing square roots, tangents, and double-angles looks like an absolute nightmare. But with one clever trigonometric identity and a smooth u-substitution, the entire problem collapses perfectly! 

In this video, we break down how to evaluate the indefinite integral of sqrt(tan(x)) / sin(2x) step-by-step. 

💡 THE CALCULUS TRICK USED:
We use the double-angle identity sin(2x) = 2*sin(x)*cos(x). By multiplying the numerator and denominator by cos(x) (or dividing by cos^2(x)), we transform the entire integrand into terms of sec^2(x) and tan(x). This sets up a perfect u-substitution where u = tan(x) and du = sec^2(x) dx!

We introduce the cofactor expansion definition of the determinant of a square matrix of any size, also called the Laplace Expansion. This recursive definition involves two new terms: minors and cofactors. The minor, Mij, of the entry aij is the determinant of the submatrix remaining when the ith row and jth column are deleted. Then, the cofactor of the entry aij is (-1)^(i+j)*Mij. We'll do an example of finding all cofactors of a 2x2 matrix and using the cofactor expansion to find the determinant of the 2x2 matrix, then we will use the cofactor expansion to find the determinant of a 3x3 matrix along a row and then along a column. #linearalgebra

This is a complete, beginner-friendly tour of the notation behind machine learning.
You'll learn the summation Σ and product Π (they're just for-loops), subscripts vs
superscripts, the partial derivative ∂ and the gradient ∇, expectation 𝔼, argmin,
integrals, the grammar symbols (∈ ∀ ∃ ≈ ∝), blackboard letters like ℝⁿ that tell you
an object's shape, the Greek-letter conventions papers rely on (θ, η, λ…), probability
notation (the "given" bar, the bell curve 𝒩, KL divergence), linear-algebra typography
(bold = vector), and big-O — then we decode a real formula, the mean squared error,
into one plain English sentence. No hard math. Just translation.

title: Basis and Components Explained Visually | Why u = ui ei?
description:
What are the basis and components of a vector?

A vector is the actual geometric object. Its components are the numbers used to describe that vector in a chosen basis.

If e1, e2, e3 form a basis, then any vector u can be written as

u = u1 e1 + u2 e2 + u3 e3

Using Einstein summation notation, this becomes

u = ui ei

where repeated index i is summed.

Key idea:

Basis vectors give directions.
Components give amounts.
The vector is the weighted sum of basis directions.

A basis must satisfy two conditions:

1. The basis vectors must be linearly independent.

No nonzero combination of them should give the zero vector.

2. The basis vectors must span the space.

Their linear combinations must be able to reach every vector in the vector space.

So,

basis = independent plus spans the space

Most important tensor idea:

The vector itself is invariant.
The component list is basis-dependent.

If the basis changes, the component numbers change. But the vector u remains the same geometric object.

Memory trick:

Basis = directions.
Components = amounts.
Vector = weighted sum.

Do not confuse the vector with its component list.

title: Why does everything fall in a curve? 🎯 #learnphysics #qn #education #phys101 #physics
description:
Throw anything — a ball, a water jet, a cannonball — and it always traces the same shape: a parabola. Why? Because horizontal and vertical motion are completely independent. The sideways speed stays constant while gravity pulls down, and the two combine into a perfect curve. Launch at 45° and you get maximum range — and any two angles adding to 90° land in exactly the same place.

Full lesson: Motion in 2D | PHYS 101 Lecture 3

title: Why does a vector have components?
description:
A vector points diagonally — but the world is built from horizontal and vertical. A component is simply the vector's "shadow" along each direction: how much of it points sideways, and how much points up. Once you see it as a shadow, you never have to memorise sin and cos again — the triangle hands it to you.

title: ORGANIC CHEM DEMONSTRATION/REACTIVITY-Primary Alkyl Halides in 15% NaI in Acetone
description:
This experiment investigates the relative reactivity of primary alkyl halides through the Finkelstein reaction. A solution of sodium iodide in acetone serves as both solvent and nucleophile source, allowing iodide ions to displace other halides via an SN2 mechanism. As the reaction proceeds, insoluble sodium chloride or sodium bromide is formed, which precipitates out of solution. The formation of this precipitate provides a visual indicator of reaction progress and allows comparison of leaving group ability among alkyl halides. Faster precipitation corresponds to a better leaving group and a more favorable SN2 reaction pathway.

Done: 6/6/2026

title: Markov Chains Explained: Simulation vs Exact Probability | Weather Example & Python Tutorial
description:
How can we predict the future with a Markov Chain?

There are two powerful approaches:

🎲 Simulation — Generate one possible future path using randomness.

🧮 Matrix Multiplication — Calculate the exact probability of each state after any number of steps.

In this beginner-friendly animation, we'll use a simple weather model with Sunny and Rainy states to explore both methods.

You'll learn:

✅ What a Markov Chain simulation does

✅ Why every simulation run is different

✅ What sample paths are

✅ How transition matrices work

✅ How to calculate probabilities after 10 days

✅ Python code using NumPy

✅ Why the weather converges to a steady-state distribution

✅ The difference between "What could happen?" and "How likely is it to happen?"

By the end, you'll understand why simulation and matrix multiplication answer different questions and how both are essential tools in probability, statistics, machine learning, and data science.

Whether you're learning Markov Chains, AI, mathematics, Python, or stochastic processes, this video provides an intuitive visual explanation of one of the most important concepts in modeling uncertain systems.

title: Witness Removals Stable #codingcontest #codechef #codingtutorial #codingasmr #codinglife #python
description:
In competitive programming, "upsolving" means to solve problems after a contest has ended. It's a practice used to improve problem-solving skills by tackling problems that were not solved during the contest.  

DISPART (Leave No Witnesses)
Every power-of-2 position (1, 2, 4, 8, ...) is forced to contain 1.
Every position that has no larger supermask within [1, N] is forced to contain 0.
If N itself is a power of 2, the answer is -1 because the highest power of 2 is forced to be both 1 and 0.
For each position, check whether it violates its forced value and count the required flips.
Final answer = total number of positions that need flipping.

Restricted Removals
An element can be deleted only if its current position matches a position in B with the same value.
After every deletion, the array is re-indexed, so elements can move left.
Only the last occurrence of 0 and 1 in B matters (last0 and last1).
Compute the effective position using:
effective_position = current_index - deleted_count
and check whether the element can reach last0 or last1.
Count all deletable elements; answer = N - deletable_elements.

Stable Diffusion (Easy)
Start by assuming every non-empty subarray is stable.
The only bad subarrays are certain long alternating patterns of 1s and 2s.
Treat every gap between adjacent elements as a center and expand outward using two pointers.
Use rem to track the depth of the alternating pattern; when rem ≥ 3, an unstable subarray is found.
Subtract all unstable subarrays from the total number of subarrays to get the final answer.

Do check the official site of python for better understanding.

title: Stop Writing Empty Comments in Python! 🛑 #python #shorts #coding #programming #learn #tutorial
description:

title: Huffman Coding Algorithm Solved Visually Step by Step | Computer Science
description:
Struggling to build a Huffman Tree and generate accurate binary codes for lossless data compression? You are certainly not alone. Calculating character frequencies, arranging leaf nodes, and assigning optimal prefix codes can be confusing without the right visual problem-solving method. This step-by-step tutorial demystifies the entire process, turning a complex greedy algorithm into an easy-to-follow visual exercise.

In this comprehensive tutorial, we break down the Huffman Coding algorithm using a detailed, visual problem-solving approach designed for computer science students. We start by calculating the frequency of each character within a given dataset, organizing these frequencies into a priority queue, and systematically merging the lowest frequency nodes. By watching the Huffman Tree grow step by step, you will understand how the greedy approach naturally assigns shorter binary codes to frequently occurring characters while allocating longer codes to rare characters. We then show you how to traverse the completed binary tree—assigning zeros to left branches and ones to right branches—to generate valid prefix codes that guarantee unambiguous decoding. Furthermore, we analyze the mathematical side of the algorithm, teaching you how to calculate the average code length, determine the total bits required for the encoded message, and compute the exact data compression ratio compared to fixed-length encoding schemes like ASCII. We also evaluate the algorithm's time complexity, explaining why using a min-heap structure results in optimal O(N log N) performance. Whether you are preparing for your CBSE Class 12 Computer Science board exams, tackling your B.Tech Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA) syllabus, or practicing numericals for the GATE examination, this guide will help you master data compression flawlessly.

What you will learn:

title: Stack vs Queue Data Structures Visually Explained | Computer Science | Computer Science
description:
Ever wondered how your web browser's back button remembers your history, or how a printer manages hundreds of incoming jobs? The secret behind these everyday technologies lies in two fundamental concepts: Stack and Queue data structures. Understanding the critical differences between LIFO and FIFO methodologies is an absolute necessity for mastering complex algorithms, acing competitive coding interviews, and building highly efficient software.

In this comprehensive visual guide, we break down exactly how stacks and queues operate within a computer's memory architecture. A stack predictably follows the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) principle, operating much like a physical stack of heavy books where the very last item placed on top is always the first one removed. In stark contrast, a queue operates on a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) basis, behaving exactly like a disciplined line of people waiting at a busy movie theater ticket counter. We will visually explore the primary operations for each structure, taking a closer look at push and pop commands for stacks, alongside enqueue and dequeue commands for queues. Grasping these essential memory management and data sequencing techniques is a mandatory stepping stone for high school students tackling their board exams, college students diving into advanced Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA), or ambitious candidates preparing for the rigorous GATE CS/IT examinations. Visualizing these traditionally abstract programming concepts on a split screen makes it incredibly easy to remember their real-world applications.

What you will learn:
- The definitive differences between Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) and First-In-First-Out (FIFO) access principles.
- How push and pop operations strictly manipulate data elements within a vertical stack environment.
- The underlying mechanics of enqueue and dequeue operations within a standard queue structure.
- Real-world applications of stacks, such as browser history navigation and software undo mechanisms.
- Essential use cases for queues, including operating system task scheduling and print spooling pipelines.
- How to visually trace the step-by-step addition and removal of elements in both memory structures.

Topics Covered:

title: Prim's Algorithm vs Kruskal's Algorithm for Maze Generation
description:
Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms are greedy methods used to find a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) in a weighted graph.

Here I've used them to generate mazes. The resulting mazes have noticeably different characteristics.

While Kruskal's algorithm produces mazes that look very natural and uniform with many short dead ends. Prim's algorithm tends to produce mazes with more straight lines and a slightly "radial" pattern growing outward from the starting point. It generates fewer, but longer, dead ends compared to Kruskal's.

At the end, BFS was used to find the shortest path for solving mazes.

Without proper timing, even the smartest processor can fail.
Because in digital design, synchronization is everything.

title: “The Tiny Switch That Powers the World | How Transistors Actually Work”
description:
Every computer, smartphone, and AI system runs on one tiny invention: the transistor.

But how can a microscopic piece of silicon control the entire digital world?

In this engineering deep dive, we explore how transistors actually work — from semiconductor physics and PN junctions to modern MOSFET architecture used inside CPUs and GPUs. You’ll see how a simple electronic switch became the foundation of modern computing.

We’ll break down:
• Semiconductor physics and doping
• PN junctions and electron flow
• Bipolar Junction Transistors (BJT)
• MOSFET transistors used in modern chips
• How billions of transistors form logic gates and processors
• Why transistor scaling enabled the computer revolution

The transistor was invented in 1947 by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley at Bell Labs, and it completely replaced vacuum tubes, enabling smaller, faster, and more powerful electronics.

Today, modern processors contain tens of billions of transistors operating at nanometer scale — powering everything from smartphones to artificial intelligence.

If you want to understand how computers really work, this is where the story begins.

title: JFET Principles: How Junction Field Effect Transistors Work
description:
JFET! Learn how this unipolar, voltage-controlled device manages current with precision.

In this technical guide, we break down the Junction Field Effect Transistor (JFET). Unlike standard bipolar transistors, JFETs use an electric field to control current, making them incredibly efficient for low-noise applications. We’ll explore the internal architecture of N-channel and P-channel types and show you exactly how the gate voltage manipulates the depletion region.

We also dive into the critical operational milestones, specifically the Pinch-off Voltage, and analyze the trade-offs between their compact size and gain-bandwidth limits. Whether you're designing a radio frequency (RF) amplifier or studying for an engineering exam, this JFET masterclass has you covered.

Key Topics Covered:

Unipolar vs. Bipolar: Why JFETs only use one type of charge carrier.

Gate-Source Control: How voltage "squeezes" the channel.

Pinch-off Explained: The moment the current stops.

N-Channel vs. P-Channel: Understanding the material differences.

Applications: RF amplification, digital switching, and Op-Amps.

title: Logarithms | Log laws, change of base, equations
description:
Welcome to Day 7 of the 50 Days of Tutelage series. Logarithms are simply the inverse of exponents. This lesson breaks down the fundamental rules of logs and shows you how to use them to solve equations where the unknown variable is an exponent.
We walk through the core concepts in a simple, step-by-step flow:
• What is a Logarithm?: Understanding the basic definition—if b^y = x, then \log_b(x) = y. We look at how to switch between exponential form and logarithmic form.
• The Core Laws of Logs: Mastering the main operational rules: the Product Rule (\log xy = \log x + \log y), the Quotient Rule (\log \frac{x}{y} = \log x - \log y), and the Power Rule (\log x^k = k \log x).
• Special Bases: Differentiating between Common Logarithms (Base 10) and Natural Logarithms (Base e, written as \ln).
• Change of Base Formula: How to rewrite a logarithm to any base so you can easily calculate or simplify it (\log_b a = \frac{\log_c a}{\log_c b}).

title: Differential Equations: What College Never Taught You
description:
What if I told you that one mathematical idea connects planetary motion, pendulums, springs, electrical circuits, population growth, fluid flow, and even the motion of galaxies?

That idea is the differential equation.

In this video, we explore the remarkable story behind differential equations, from Johannes Kepler's observations of planetary motion to Isaac Newton's invention of a mathematical framework for describing change, to Leonhard Euler's breakthrough methods for solving entire families of equations.

Along the way, we'll discover:

• Why Kepler's laws were one of the greatest mysteries in science
• How Newton derived planetary motion from a simple mathematical rule
• Why the infamous three-body problem defeated even Newton himself
• How differential equations describe motion, change, and the laws of nature
• Euler's powerful method for solving differential equations
• The mathematics behind springs, pendulums, and oscillations
• Why imaginary numbers naturally emerge in physical systems
• How simple rules can produce surprisingly complex behavior

Differential equations are often taught as a collection of formulas and techniques.
But historically, they represented something far deeper: a new way of understanding reality itself.
Instead of describing where things are, differential equations describe how things change.
And from those rules of change, entire worlds of structure emerge.

If you enjoy mathematics, physics, engineering, scientific history, or the hidden ideas that shaped our understanding of the universe, this video is for you.

Timestamps:
00:00 - The Idealized Two-Body Problem: Newton's second law meets the inverse square law.
00:43 - The Conceptual Leap: Shifting from finding unknown numbers to unknown functions.
02:52 - Newton's "Method of Fluxions": Inventing calculus at Wools Thorpe during the plague.
04:43 - Proving the Ellipse: How differential equations turned Kepler's observations into mathematical necessity.
05:43 - Rules of Motion: Visualizing equations as "fields of arrows" and the role of initial conditions.
06:39 - The Three-Body Problem: Newton’s failure to solve the "coupled system" of the Sun, Earth, and Moon.
08:39 - Leonhard Euler’s Systematic Approach: Transforming calculus into algebra.
10:14 - The Power of Exponentials: Using Euler’s formula to explain why springs and pendulums oscillate.
14:21 - Henri Poincaré and the N-Body Problem: A prize-winning memoir and a significant error.
15:15 - The Homoclinic Tangle: Discovering how intersecting manifolds lead to unpredictable complexity.
16:32 - Deterministic Chaos: Why precise laws do not always lead to predictable futures

title: Python Crash Course for Developers | Core Python You Must Know
description:
Welcome to AI & Data Skills Shorts by CodeVisium 🚀
This is a Python crash course for developers who want to understand Python deeply and practically, not just syntax — the same clarity you’d expect from a long-form course, compressed into a structured guide.

🔹 1️⃣ Variables & Data Types
📌 What this means

Python does not require type declaration.
The type is inferred at runtime.

📌 Example Explained
x = 10        # int
name = "Alex" # str


x becomes an integer automatically

name becomes a string

Type can change dynamically

📌 How developers use this

Faster prototyping

Cleaner code

Less boilerplate than Java/C++

✅ One-Liner Concept
Python → dynamically typed

🧠 Meaning

Variable type is decided at runtime, not at declaration.

🔹 2️⃣ Control Flow (if / loops)
📌 What this means

Control flow decides which code runs and how many times.

📌 Example Explained
if x v 5:
    print("Yes")


Condition is checked

Code runs only if condition is True

Loops:

for i in range(3):
    print(i)

📌 How developers use this

Business logic

Data validation

Iterating datasets

✅ One-Liner Concept
if → condition | loop → repetition

🧠 Meaning

Decisions + repetition drive program logic.

🔹 3️⃣ Functions
📌 What this means

Functions group logic into reusable units.

📌 Example Explained
def add(a, b):
    return a + b


def defines a function

Arguments go inside parentheses

return sends result back

📌 How developers use this

Clean architecture

Code reuse

Testing & debugging

✅ One-Liner Concept
function → input → logic → output

🧠 Meaning

Functions turn inputs into outputs predictably.

🔹 4️⃣ Data Structures
📌 What this means

Data structures store and organize data.

📌 Example Explained
nums = [1, 2, 3]


Common structures:

list → ordered, mutable

tuple → ordered, immutable

set → unique items

dict → key-value pairs

Example:

user = {"name": "Alex", "age": 25}

📌 How developers use this

Handling APIs

Managing application state

Processing datasets

✅ One-Liner Concept
list | tuple | set | dict → data containers

🧠 Meaning

Choose structure based on data behavior.

🔹 5️⃣ Modules & Libraries
📌 What this means

Python allows importing built-in and external code.

📌 Example Explained
import math
math.sqrt(16)


math is a built-in module

External libraries add new capabilities

Install external libraries:

pip install requests


Import them:

import requests

📌 How developers use this

Avoid reinventing the wheel

Build faster

Scale applications

✅ One-Liner Concept
import → reuse existing code

🧠 Meaning

Libraries turn Python into a powerful ecosystem.

🧠 Interview Questions & Answers
Q1. What does dynamic typing mean in Python?

→ Variable type is determined at runtime.

Q2. Difference between list and tuple?

→ List is mutable, tuple is immutable.

Q3. Why are functions important?

→ Code reuse and clean architecture.

Q4. What is a module in Python?

→ A file containing reusable Python code.

Q5. How do you install external libraries?

→ Using pip install library_name.

title: SQL Interview Question: Find Customers Who Have Never Made a Purchase | LEFT JOIN Explained
description:
🚀 SQL Interview Question Series

In this video, you'll learn how to find customers who have never made a purchase using SQL.

Question:
Find customers who have not made any purchase.

We'll cover:
✅ LEFT JOIN Explained
✅ Why NULL appears after a LEFT JOIN
✅ Using WHERE IS NULL to find missing records
✅ Common SQL Interview Trap
✅ Difference Between "No Purchase" and "Purchased Once"
✅ Real Interview Examples

SQL Query:

SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN sales s
ON c.customer_id = s.customer_id
WHERE s.sale_id IS NULL;

💡 Interview Tip:
Whenever you need to find records that don't have a matching record in another table, think:

LEFT JOIN + IS NULL

This pattern is commonly called an Anti Join and is frequently asked in SQL interviews.

"How to Read a Single Observation From Multiple Lines of Raw Data | SAS Tutorial in English - Part 15

Welcome to Part 15 of our step-by-step SAS Training series! In the last video, we looked at handling packed lines with the Double Trailing @. In this session, we tackle the exact opposite problem: what do you do when a single customer's or entity's information is spread over 2, 3, or more rows in your text file?

In this video, we break down the 3 different ways to handle multiple raw records per observation in simple English:
✅ Method 1: Multiple INPUT Statements – How using sequential INPUT statements automatically forces SAS to advance to the next line of data.
✅ Method 2: The Forward Slash (/) Line Pointer – How to use the relative line pointer control to skip directly to the next raw data record.
✅ Method 3: The Absolute Line Pointer (#n) – How to navigate to any specific row n within a single observation block (e.g., #2 Age 3.).
✅ Comparison: When to choose which method based on the structure and complexity of your raw file.

SIBO GIT Breath Test - Fructose Panel Collection Instructions
description:
Getting ready to complete your SIBO GIT Breath Test – Fructose Panel? This step-by-step guide walks you through everything you need to know to collect your breath samples correctly and get the most accurate results possible.

Accurate test results start with a properly collected specimen — watch this full walkthrough before you begin.

📋 QUICK REFERENCE – COLLECTION SCHEDULE
Sample 1: 8:00 AM (Baseline — before drinking solution)
Sample 2: 8:20 AM
Sample 3: 8:40 AM
Sample 4: 9:00 AM
Sample 5: 9:30 AM
Sample 6: 10:00 AM (Stop here for 2-hour collection)
Sample 7: 10:30 AM
Sample 8: 11:00 AM (Stop here for 3-hour collection)


✅ KEY REMINDERS BEFORE YOU START
🗓️ 2–4 Weeks Before: Wait at least 4 weeks after a colonoscopy or barium enema, and 2–4 weeks after antibiotics, antifungals, or Pepto-Bismol.
📅 7 Days Before: Avoid laxatives, stool softeners, stool bulking agents, and antacids containing aluminum or magnesium hydroxide.
🥗 24 Hours Before: Eat only approved foods — baked/broiled chicken, fish, or turkey (salt & pepper only), white bread, plain steamed white rice, eggs, clear broth, water, plain coffee, or black tea. Vegetarians may have tofu with salt and pepper. Do NOT take probiotics.
⏰ 12 Hours Before: Begin fasting. No food or drink except water. Hold non-essential medications and supplements unless directed by your physician. No gum, candy, or mouthwash.
🚭 1 Hour Before: No smoking (including secondhand smoke), no sleeping, and no vigorous exercise. Do not use toothpaste.

⚠️ IMPORTANT NOTES
Do NOT open, loosen, or remove the caps on your collection tubes — this breaks the vacuum seal and will ruin your sample.
Do NOT stick your finger into the mouthpiece — there is a sharp needle inside.
Do NOT drink water for 1 hour after consuming the fructose solution.
LABEL ALL TUBES with your first name, last name, and tube number (1–6 or 1–8).
Do not collect during an acute illness.
Fructose solution should be used with caution by diabetics or those with a history of adverse/allergic reactions.

📦 SHIPPING YOUR SAMPLE
Once all tubes are collected and labeled, place the completed requisition form in the outside pocket of the Biohazard Bag, seal your tubes in the bubblewrap and Biohazard Bag, place inside the provided shipping envelope, and ship using the prepaid label. Note your tracking number for reference.
Results are available within 8–10 business days and delivered directly to your provider portal.

🔬 About This Test
The SIBO GIT Breath Test – Fructose Panel is a non-invasive assessment that measures hydrogen and methane gas production to evaluate small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) and fructose malabsorption. Testing is performed using the QuinTron BreathTracker with solid-state sensors and CO₂ normalization for precise, clinically actionable results.

description:
In this lecture, we explore the important Operating System concepts of *Processes and Threads* for 10th Class Computer Science (Punjab Board 2026).
Playlist English Medium: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLFVfaTjQLabXZJU4aqq1knqdrPV8JNdxN
Playlist Urdu Medium: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLFVfaTjQLabVowEA9GtJTX0rzTUzhugq7
You will learn:
• What is a Process?
• What is a Thread?
• Differences between Process and Thread
• Process Memory and Resource Management
• Multithreading Concept
• Advantages and Disadvantages of Threads
• Process vs Thread Comparison
• Real-Life Examples of Processes and Threads
• MCQs and Examination-Oriented Notes

A process is a program in execution, while a thread is a smaller unit of execution within a process. Threads share resources and memory, making them faster and more efficient for multitasking, whereas processes operate independently with separate memory spaces. Understanding these concepts is essential for learning how modern operating systems manage tasks and improve performance.

This lecture is designed according to the latest Punjab Board Computer Science syllabus and helps students prepare for board examinations through simple explanations and practical examples.

description:
Operating System Quiz: How to increase a process scheduling capacity or process priority in Linux and Unix systems? Test your knowledge of core computer science and Linux administration concepts in this quick 8-second OS quiz! 

In this video, we look at an essential operating system multiple-choice question (MCQ) that frequently appears in university engineering exams, GATE CS preparation, and DevOps or Linux System Administrator interviews. 

 can you guess the correct answer before the timer runs out? The question is: How do you increase or change a process scheduling capacity? 
The options provided are:
A) nice
B) fair
C) renice
D) top

Watch the full short to see the correct answer explained! Understanding how CPU scheduling algorithms, process management, and kernel prioritization work is fundamental for anyone learning computer science, Linux shell scripting, or system architecture.

💡 KEY TOPICS COVERED IN THIS SHORT & DESCRIPTION:
- Operating System tutorial for beginners and computer science students.

Whether you are preparing for a tech interview, studying for an IT certification, or just brushing up on your Linux command-line skills, this quick quiz is designed to help you practice on the go. The nice command is used to launch a new process with a specific scheduling priority, which modifies how the kernel allocates CPU time slices to that particular task. Lowering the nice value increases the process priority, giving it more scheduling capacity on the system!

description:
# VLSM Subnetting Explained Step by Step | Variable Length Subnet Masking

In this lesson, we explore Variable Length Subnet Masking (VLSM), an advanced subnetting technique that allows network administrators to allocate IP address space efficiently based on the actual requirements of different departments or network segments.

Unlike Fixed Length Subnet Masking (FLSM), where every subnet is the same size, VLSM creates subnets of different sizes, reducing address wastage and improving network utilization.

This tutorial demonstrates the complete VLSM process using a practical case study involving departmental network allocation. You will learn how to determine subnet sizes, allocate address ranges, calculate network and broadcast addresses, and build efficient addressing schemes for real-world networks.

title: History Repeats Itself | Dark History Documentary
description:
🔥 HUMAN NATURE REVEALED IN HISTORY! 🔥

In the vast expanse of human history, a peculiar phenomenon has been observed: the repetition of historical events. Ancient Western thinkers like Cicero, Seneca, and Aristotle noted the cyclical nature of civilizations, comparing their rise and fall to the life cycle of a person. This metaphor resurfaced in the 19th-century writings of Herbert Spencer and Émile Durkheim, who also observed the inevitability of historical patterns. Meanwhile, Eastern thought expressed a similar idea through the Mandate of Heaven, which held that unjust rulers would inevitably lose divine support and be overthrown.

The shocking truth is that history does indeed repeat itself, not in exact repetition, but in recognizable cycles and analogies that persist across ages. This phenomenon has been famously asserted by George Santayana, who said that “history repeats itself,” a sentiment echoed in popular aphorisms such as Mark Twain’s observation that “history doesn’t repeat itself, but it does rhyme.” The escalation of historical events, the rise and fall of empires, and the persistence of human nature all point to a deeper truth about the human condition.

The philosophical lesson that can be gleaned from this phenomenon is that human nature remains a constant, despite the changing times and circumstances. The same desires and passions that drove ancient civilizations to greatness and destruction are still present today, shaping the course of human events. This realization should prompt us to reflect on our own place in the grand narrative of history and to consider the wisdom of those who have come before us. As we navigate the complexities of our own time, we would do well to remember that history is not just a series of dusty relics, but a living, breathing guide to the human condition.

description:
Welcome to Mini History. A fresh look on Ancient History's most fascinating tales!

He crossed the known world—and changed how Europe understood it forever.

In 1271 AD, a seventeen-year-old Venetian merchant stepped onto a wooden pier and sailed east—toward deserts that sang, cities larger than any Europe had known, and an empire that ruled half the earth.

This is the true story of Marco Polo.

From the markets of Venice to the court of Kublai Khan, Marco Polo spent 24 years crossing deserts, oceans, and empires—serving the Mongol court, witnessing inventions centuries ahead of Europe, and recording a world that many would refuse to believe existed.

Captured in war and imprisoned, he dictated his memories into a book that would reshape maps, ignite imaginations, and inspire explorers for centuries—including Christopher Columbus.

This episode explores:
 • The Silk Road and the Mongol Empire at its height
 • Cities of unimaginable scale and wealth
 • Paper money, coal, porcelain, and global trade networks
 • Why Marco Polo was called a liar—and why history proved him right
 • How one traveler stitched East and West together with words

Discovery is not about arriving somewhere new…
It’s about returning changed.

title: Fall Asleep to the ENTIRE Story of Atlantis
description:
Atlantis is one of history’s most enduring mysteries—a legendary lost civilization first described by the Greek philosopher Plato in the 4th century BCE. According to his account, Atlantis was a mighty island kingdom beyond the Pillars of Hercules, rich in resources, advanced in knowledge, and powerful enough to challenge the known world. But in a single catastrophic day and night, it supposedly sank beneath the waves, leaving nothing but myth behind. For centuries, scholars, explorers, and dreamers have debated whether Atlantis was a real place, a moral allegory, or a mixture of both. Some link it to the Minoans of Crete, others to distant lands across the Atlantic, while modern theories see it as a timeless parable about hubris and the fall of civilizations. In this episode, we explore the legend, theories, and legacy of Atlantis—the city that may never have existed, yet continues to captivate the imagination of the world.

title: The Entire History of Germany
description:
#germany #history #documentary 

Thanks to Storyblocks for sponsoring this video! Get 2 extra months free with annual plans for a limited-time only: https://storyblocks.com/ThisIsHistory

WATCH THIS AND ALL OUR VIDEOS OVER ON SPOTIFY: https://open.spotify.com/show/4ONNqWZ8qsl6DIyIp0uR8s?si=a444627f2aa343d7

WATCH THIS AND ALL OUR VIDEOS COMPLETELY AD-FREE OVER ON OUR SUBSTACK: https://thisishistory.substack.com/?r=2zq5ao&utm_campaign=pub-share-checklist

The concept of Germany as a distinct region in Central Europe can be traced to Julius Caesar, who referred to the unconquered area east of the Rhine as Germania, thus distinguishing it from Gaul. The victory of the Germanic tribes in the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest (AD 9) prevented annexation by the Roman Empire, although the Roman provinces of Germania Superior and Germania Inferior were established along the Rhine. Following the Fall of the Western Roman Empire, the Franks conquered the other West Germanic tribes. When the Frankish Empire was divided among Charles the Great's heirs in 843, the eastern part became East Francia, and later Kingdom of Germany. In 962, Otto I became the first Holy Roman Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire, the medieval German state.

During the High Middle Ages, the Hanseatic League, dominated by German port cities, established itself along the Baltic and North Seas. The development of a crusading element within German Christendom led to the State of the Teutonic Order along the Baltic coast in what would later become Prussia. In the Investiture Controversy, the German Emperors resisted Catholic Church authority. In the Late Middle Ages, the regional dukes, princes, and bishops gained power at the expense of the emperors. Martin Luther led the Protestant Reformation within the Catholic Church after 1517, as the northern and eastern states became Protestant, while most of the southern and western states remained Catholic. The Thirty Years' War, a civil war from 1618 to 1648 brought tremendous destruction to the Holy Roman Empire. The estates of the empire attained great autonomy in the Peace of Westphalia, the most important being Austria, Prussia, Bavaria and Saxony. With the Napoleonic Wars, feudalism fell away and the Holy Roman Empire was dissolved in 1806. Napoleon established the Confederation of the Rhine as a German puppet state, but after the French defeat, the German Confederation was established under Austrian presidency. The German revolutions of 1848–1849 failed but the Industrial Revolution modernized the German economy, leading to rapid urban growth and the emergence of the socialist movement. Prussia, with its capital Berlin, grew in power. German universities became world-class centres for science and humanities, while music and art flourished. The unification of Germany was achieved under the leadership of the Chancellor Otto von Bismarck with the formation of the German Empire in 1871. The new Reichstag, an elected parliament, had only a limited role in the imperial government. Germany joined the other powers in colonial expansion in Africa and the Pacific.

By 1900, Germany was the dominant power on the European continent and its rapidly expanding industry had surpassed Britain's while provoking it in a naval arms race. Germany led the Central Powers in World War I, but was defeated, partly occupied, forced to pay war reparations, and stripped of its colonies and significant territory along its borders. The German Revolution of 1918–1919 ended the German Empire with the abdication of Wilhelm II and established the Weimar Republic, an ultimately unstable parliamentary democracy. In January 1933, Adolf Hitler, leader of the Nazi Party, used the economic hardships of the Great Depression along with popular resentment over the terms imposed on Germany at the end of World War I to establish a totalitarian regime. Germany quickly remilitarized, annexed its German-speaking neighbours and invaded Poland, triggering World War II. By 1944, the German Army was pushed back on all fronts until finally collapsing in May 1945. Under occupation by the Allies, denazification efforts took place, large populations under former German-occupied territories were displaced, German territories were split up by the victorious powers and in the east annexed by Poland and the Soviet Union. Germany spent the entirety of the Cold War era divided into the NATO-aligned West Germany and Warsaw Pact-aligned East Germany. 

In 1989, the Berlin Wall was opened, the Eastern Bloc collapsed, and East and West Germany were reunited in 1990. The Franco-German friendship became the basis for the political integration of Western Europe in the European Union. In 1998–1999, Germany was one of the founding countries of the eurozone and remains one of the economic powerhouses on the continent.

title: Fall Asleep to the ENTIRE History of The Silk Road
description:
The Silk Road was the vast network of trade routes that connected East and West for over a thousand years, shaping the course of global history. Stretching from China through Central Asia to the Mediterranean, it carried not only silk, spices, and precious goods but also ideas, religions, technologies, and cultures that transformed civilizations. Caravans of merchants and explorers braved deserts, mountains, and bandits, while great cities like Samarkand, Kashgar, and Constantinople thrived as hubs of exchange. Along these routes, Buddhism spread to China, paper-making reached the West, and countless innovations crossed continents. More than a highway of commerce, the Silk Road was the world’s first true information superhighway, weaving together distant peoples and laying the groundwork for globalization. In this episode, we journey along the Silk Road—where trade, culture, and history converged across thousands of miles.

description:
The story of Mesopotamia, often called the cradle of civilization, begins over 5,000 years ago in the fertile lands between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, where humanity first transformed from scattered farming communities into complex urban societies. From the Sumerians, who built the first cities, invented writing, and raised monumental ziggurats, to the Akkadians, Babylonians, and Assyrians who forged vast empires, Mesopotamia was the birthplace of countless innovations—law codes, astronomy, mathematics, irrigation, and literature like the Epic of Gilgamesh. It was here that kings ruled over city-states, gods were worshiped in grand temples, and trade connected distant parts of the ancient world. Yet Mesopotamia was also a land of constant struggle, plagued by wars, shifting powers, and the unpredictable floods of its rivers. Over millennia, its civilizations rose and fell, leaving behind clay tablets and ruins that still whisper the dawn of human society. In this episode, we explore the entire history of Mesopotamia—the world’s first true civilization, where history itself began.

In 1920, Ludwig von Mises changed the debate on socialism forever. He didn't argue about corruption or laziness; he focused on the "Economic Calculation Problem." Without private property and market prices, how does a planner know what to build, how much to make, or where to send resources?

title: Cambridge Economics National Income: GDP, Growth And GDP Per Head
description:
Cambridge Economics national income is a key topic for understanding how countries measure growth, living standards and the success of macroeconomic policies. This video explains the difference between GDP, real GDP, economic growth and GDP per head, with a focus on the precise wording students need for stronger marks.

The lesson shows why economic growth must be defined as an increase in real GDP over time, not simply as more output. It also explains how GDP per head is calculated by dividing total GDP by the total population, helping students avoid common mistakes in multiple-choice and written questions.

Students also see how to build a full cause-and-effect chain for analysis questions, using investment, aggregate demand, technology, productivity, costs, prices and output. The discussion then moves into balanced evaluation, asking whether lower GDP is always a disadvantage by considering unemployment, incomes, tax revenue, pollution, inflation, natural resources and population changes. History documentary exploring the causes and events of war. The Economic Web: How Spain's Civil War Unfolded
The Spanish Civil War was a complex web of economic interests, with fascist leader Francisco Franco backed by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy. But the war was also driven by territorial disputes over Catalonia and the Mediterranean. Power struggles between regional factions fueled the conflict. As fascist forces closed in, the Republican government's economic policies were deemed too radical. The resulting power vacuum was filled by the Nationalists, who would go on to dominate Spanish politics for decades. Follow for the next cause explained.

title: 1 Intro to NAVIGATIONAL MIND unscripted: KINETICS, KONSTELLATION & KEDOS #hippocampus #philosophy
description:
#navigational #philosophy #mind INTRODUCTION: #KINETICS #KONSTELLATION #KEDOS
Navigational Approach to Mind
As an exploration of the mind through the lens of embodied science, the Navigational Philosophy of Mind presents a novel approach to understanding our consciousness. Unlike traditional computational models, this perspective emphasizes the mind as a navigational system, informed by three interconnected principles: Kinetics, Konstellation, and Kedos.

Three K's: Foundations of Navigational Mind:
Hi, everyone. Welcome to an insightful journey into the 'Three K’s'—Kinetics, Konstellation, and Kedos. These concepts are integral to the navigational approach to embodied science and cognition, a field that redefines how we perceive and study the mind.

Our aim is to move beyond traditional frameworks that have historically focused on binary oppositions—either computational or connectionist models—and towards a more fluid understanding. This introductory discussion provides an overview of these ideas, setting the stage for a more in-depth exploration through a series of videos and writings.

Kinetics: The Movement of Mind

Kinetics, familiar to many as movement, serves as the first cornerstone of our navigational approach. Consider the myriad movements around and within us: the dance of trees in the breeze, the stirrings of life within our own bodies, and the ceaseless dance of molecules and atoms. By framing the mind as a series of movements, we simplify our understanding of a wide variety of life forms. This kinetic perspective helps us transcend binary thinking, offering a unifying theme for the multiplicities of thought and existence.

Konstellation: From Binary to A System of Stars

The second principle, Konstellation, encourages us to shift from binary thinking to a constellation-like view. Rather than focusing on opposites, a Konstellation includes multiple points of view and relational positions. By visualizing our world as a constellation—a network of interrelated parts—each position yields different oppositions and insights. This perspective empowers us to think in dimensions beyond the linear, embracing the complexities of 3D, 4D, or even 5D perspectives in understanding our mind and philosophies.

Kedos: The Primordial Urge 

Finally, we delve into Kedos, or care, representing the physical and emotional pull at the heart of our inquiry into the mind. This complex term embodies concern, love, and the foundational urge that drives our quest for knowledge. In understanding Kedos as the ontological essence of life’s movements, we capture the dynamic tension between need and fulfillment. As a verb, Kedos signifies action—a compelling force of connection and creation within the constellation framework.

Holding Paradox into a New Way of Thinking

The navigational philosophy of mind invites us to move beyond our traditional, often constrictive viewpoints. By emphasizing movement, relational networks, and care, this approach offers a more expansive and inclusive understanding of knowing and being. When we listen to multiple voices within the Konstellation, we gain new perspectives that can lead us to healthier, more supportive ways of living.

As we embark on this journey together, consider the ways these principles might transform your own understanding of mind and meaning. The introductory video series linked below will delve into each of these principles in greater depth: 

1. **Kinetics**: Exploring the movement as a foundation for understanding the mind.
2. **Konstellation**: Embracing the multi-dimensional networks of knowledge.
3. **Kedos**: Examining care as the fundamental urge for understanding.

I invite you to engage with these ideas, share your thoughts, and follow along for more philosophical insights into the way our world navigates consciousness. As we constellate with care and curiosity, we shape new pathways for thought and connection. Let’s explore these together—watch, reflect, and discover. Stay curious, stay connected.

title: Being and Logos - Introduction to Middle-Platonism - 2 of X - The Old Academy, pt 1
description:
Welcome to Being & Logos - An Introduction to Middle-Platonism

While Plotinus and his inheritors are often associated with western mysticism and the occult philosophy, the philosophical ferment of the centuries following the Old Academy (post 347 bce) most directly influenced Hermeticism, Gnosticism, Hellenistic Magic and Astrology, Alexandrian Judaism and early Christianity.  This period of philosophy, denoted as “Middle Platonism,” is thus crucially important for the study of the development Western Esotericism and, surprisingly (or not), this period is woefully unappreciated.  This seminar aims to be an introduction to Middle-Platonism (c. 100 bce - c. 200 ce), specifically with an eye toward developments in metaphysics.  Along with deepening our appreciation of the development of western philosophy, my hope is that we come to better appreciate the philosophical dimensions of Hermeticism, Gnosticism, Hellenistic Magic and Astrology, Alexandrian Judaism, early Christianity, Neo-Platonism and Western Esotericism more widely.

title: Being and Logos - Introduction to Middle-Platonism - 1 of X - The Shadow of Plato
description:
Welcome to Being & Logos - An Introduction to Middle-Platonism

While Plotinus and his inheritors are often associated with western mysticism and the occult philosophy, the philosophical ferment of the centuries following the Old Academy (post 347 bce) most directly influenced Hermeticism, Gnosticism, Hellenistic Magic and Astrology, Alexandrian Judaism and early Christianity.  This period of philosophy, denoted as “Middle Platonism,” is thus crucially important for the study of the development Western Esotericism and, surprisingly (or not), this period is woefully unappreciated.  This seminar aims to be an introduction to Middle-Platonism (c. 100 bce - c. 200 ce), specifically with an eye toward developments in metaphysics.  Along with deepening our appreciation of the development of western philosophy, my hope is that we come to better appreciate the philosophical dimensions of Hermeticism, Gnosticism, Hellenistic Magic and Astrology, Alexandrian Judaism, early Christianity, Neo-Platonism and Western Esotericism more widely.

Welcome to Being & Logos - An Introduction to Middle-Platonism

title: An Introduction to Plato | Forms, Sophists & the Birth of Western Philosophy | Episode 01
description:
"All of Western philosophy is but a footnote to Plato." — Alfred North Whitehead

This is Episode 01 of Through the Critical Eye — a lecture series by Madani Chems Eddine's Critique. We begin where Western philosophy begins: with Plato.

Who was Plato, and why does his shadow still fall over everything we think, read, and argue about? In this lecture, we introduce the man, his world, and the ideas that made him inescapable — from the Theory of Forms to his war with the Sophists.

What we cover:
→ Plato's life: student of Socrates, teacher of Aristotle, founder of the Academy
→ The Theory of Forms — why the material world is imperfect, mutable, and second-best
→ The Diagram vs. the Proof — geometry as a path to eternal truth
→ Plato vs. the Sophists — why he feared rhetoric and what he built to defeat it
→ Key concepts: Eidos, Idealism, Doxa, Episteme, Mimesis
→ Plato's legacy from Neoplatonism to Romanticism

Next session: Book X of The Republic — Plato's attack on poetry and the banishment of the poets.

title: Marshmallow Test Misunderstood for 50 Years #debunked #science #shorts
description:
Most people believe the famous Marshmallow Test proved that successful people have more self-control. But Prof. Jiang Xueqin argues that the experiment reveals something much deeper: trust.

In this psychology Short, Prof. Jiang explains why children from stable environments may wait for the second marshmallow, while children facing uncertainty often make a rational decision to take the reward immediately. The lesson isn't simply about delayed gratification—it's about trust, authority, poverty, and how life experiences shape decision-making.

Based on one of the most famous psychology experiments ever conducted, this clip challenges conventional thinking about success, self-control, and human behavior.
This video is based on lectures by Prof. Jiang Xueqin, where we extract and simplify key ideas from long-form discussions into short, focused videos.

title: From Timeline To Threads: How Civics Really Works
description:
A timeline can tell you what happened. It can’t always tell you what it meant, or why the meaning keeps changing.

We’ve spent months building a foundation in civics: the Declaration of Independence and its claims about equality, unalienable rights, and consent; the Constitution and its structure; and the core mechanics of American government like separation of powers, checks and balances, federalism, and the rule of law. We’ve followed those ideas as they collide with reality through Supreme Court cases, political parties, and moments of national crisis from the early republic through the modern presidency. But there’s a problem with treating political history as a straight line: the closer you are to events, the harder it is to separate reaction from impact.

So we’re making a deliberate shift. Instead of racing forward president by president, we’re slowing down and pulling on threads that cut across time, focusing on the people, relationships, and recurring conflicts that reveal how power actually works. Expect episodes that lean into historical drama and civic insight: iconic rivalries like Hamilton vs Burr, the complicated bond between Adams and Jefferson, the politics of image around figures like Jackie Kennedy, and stories that sit outside the spotlight but reshape civic life. We’ll also widen the lens with themes like Juneteenth and gerrymandering through place and geography, while building toward a big question that ties the whole project together: what does the Declaration mean 250 years later?

If you want civic education that helps you make sense of the present, not just memorize the past, come with us into this next phase. Subscribe, share the show with a friend, and leave a review telling us which rivalry or overlooked figure you want us to cover next.

title: Grade 9 Civics & Government | Comparative Governments | Democracy, Monarchy & Dictatorship Explained
description:
In this Grade 9 Civics & Government lesson, students explore how different types of governments work around the world. The video introduces comparative government, helping learners understand how political systems organize power, make decisions, and protect citizens’ rights.

We begin by defining government and why societies need it — to create order, provide services, and ensure justice. Then we compare major government types:

Democracy, where people rule through elections and participation

Monarchy, where power is held by a king or queen

Dictatorship, where authority is controlled by one leader or small group

Oligarchy and Theocracy, where religion or elite groups influence rule

Students will explore real-world examples like the United States (democracy), Saudi Arabia (monarchy), and North Korea (dictatorship) to see how power and freedoms differ.

We also discuss how governments handle laws, economic policies, and citizen involvement. Learners discover that while systems vary, all share one purpose — maintaining stability and serving the people.

By the end, students will:
✅ Identify and compare major forms of government
✅ Understand how leadership and power differ globally
✅ Analyze the advantages and challenges of each system
✅ Appreciate the importance of citizen participation

This topic builds global awareness and critical thinking, showing how every nation’s system reflects its history, culture, and values.

description: In this video, I walk through Practice Problem #97, a polynomial functions question involving the Factor Theorem and synthetic division. I begin by using the given factor, (x - 3), to identify one of the zeros of the polynomial. Next, I apply synthetic division to divide the polynomial by (x - 3) and obtain a quadratic expression. title: SAT Linear Equations Question 18: Solve 6x + 5 = 41 #satmath #digitalsat #usa
description:
Can you solve this SAT linear equation in one try?

Question:
If 6x + 5 = 41, what is x?

A. 5
B. 6
C. 7
D. 8

✅ Correct Answer: B. 6

Quick Solution:
6x + 5 = 41
6x = 41 − 5
6x = 36
x = 36 ÷ 6
x = 6

This is a beginner SAT linear equations question. It tests SAT algebra, solve for x, two-step equations, and one-variable equations. These equation-solving skills are important for Digital SAT Math practice, high school algebra, and SAT prep USA students.

description:

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Q1. The line x + 3y = 7 is reflected across the line x = 0 (y-axis). What is the equation of the image?
✅ Answer: C. x + 3y = -7
💡 When a line is reflected across the y-axis, the x term changes its sign. So, x + 3y = 7 becomes -x + 3y = 7, which can be rewritten as x + 3y = -7.

Q2. A circle with its center at (1, 2) and a radius of 2 is reflected across the line x = 0 (y-axis). What are the coordinates of the center of the image?
✅ Answer: B. (-1, 2)
💡 To reflect a point across the y-axis, we change the sign of the x-coordinate. So, (1, 2) becomes (-1, 2). The y-coordinate remains the same.

Q3. The line 2x - 4y = 5 is reflected across the line y = x. What is the equation of the image?
✅ Answer: B. 2y - 4x = -5
💡 To reflect a line across the line y = x, we replace x with y and y with x in the original equation. So, 2x - 4y = 5 becomes 2y - 4x = 5. However, since the coefficients are not 1, the equation needs to be adjusted to maintain the same slope, resulting in 2y - 4x = -5.

Q4. The line 3x + 2y = 7 is reflected across the line y = 2x. What is the equation of the reflected line?
✅ Answer: B. 2x - 3y = 7
💡 To reflect the line across y = 2x, we first need to find the slope of the line. The slope of the given line is -3/2. The slope of the reflected line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the line of reflection, which is -1/2. Using this information and the fact that the line of reflection is the perpendicular bisector of the line segment connecting the original line and the reflected line, we can find the equation of the reflected line.

Q1. The vertices of a triangle are (2, 4), (6, 4), and (4, 8). What is the image of the triangle after it is reflected across the line x = 4?
✅ Answer: B. (6, 4), (2, 4), (4, 8)
💡 When reflecting across the line x = 4, the x-coordinates of the vertices that are not on the line of reflection are swapped with respect to the line. So (2, 4) becomes (6, 4), and (6, 4) becomes (2, 4). The point (4, 8) remains the same since it is on the line of reflection.

title: C Add9 and Cmaj9 Are NOT The Same Chord 🎸
description:
C Add9 and Cmaj9 might look similar on paper, but they're actually two different chords.

The secret?

A Major 9 chord MUST contain a Major 7.

An Add9 chord simply adds the 9th to a major chord without adding the 7th.

In this lesson you'll learn:

• What a 9 actually is  
• Why the 9 is the same note as the 2  
• How to quickly build a C Add9 chord  
• How to build a C Major 9 chord  
• The one note that separates them  
• When you might choose one over the other

Remember:

C Add9 = C, E, G, D

Cmaj9 = C, E, G, B, D

You can't have a Major 9 without the Major 7.

title: Compose Effective Chord Progressions… even if you don’t know theory (Counterpoint for Composers)
description:
▶ Start the free course: https://www.uremusic.com/audiation-inner-ear-training-for-musicians How to write counterpoint in four voices — all five species, applied to the SATB ensemble that sits underneath almost every chorale, fugue, and orchestral score in Western music. Full course here: https://www.uremusic.com/counterpoint-for-composers

🎹 Piano Volume: The piano in this recording is intentionally mixed low, as this course is meant to be taken after developing audiation skills. Don't turn up your speakers — instead, use what you hear as a starting point and try to complete the sound internally. That internal hearing is the skill we're building. 

This is Lecture 12 of Counterpoint for Composers, a 24‑lecture course for writers who already have two‑ and three‑part species under their belt. We start with why four parts are the foundational texture — the “conversation among four people” analogy runs through the whole lesson — then move into the mechanics: the six voice‑pairs you must check on every beat, SATB ranges and spacing, doubling, and the leading‑tone trap.

From there we walk species by species:
• First species (note‑against‑note)
• Second species (two‑against‑one with passing tones)
• Third species (four‑against‑one)
• Fourth species (suspensions, including the chain — one of the most beautiful sounds in tonal music)
• Fifth species (florid)

We close with combining species across voices, voice independence, texture and balance, an eight‑step writing workflow, and two complete worked examples — one with the cantus in the bass, one with the cantus in the soprano.

By the end, you’ll have a reliable workflow for writing four‑part counterpoint and the error‑checking habits to keep it clean.

title: The Circle of 5ths #music #piano #musictheory #musiclessons #tutorial #pianolessons #chords #keys
description:
The Circle of 5ths is helpful for understanding scales, key signatures and chords. 

The notes of the circle are Perfect 5ths apart when moving clockwise. Starting at C with no sharps or flats, one sharp is added to each key signature going forward.  

When moving counter clockwise, the notes are 4ths apart and one flat is added on to each key signature.

title: Can You Learn Piano From a Song With NO Piano in It?
channelName: Jason Zac - Nathaniel School of Music
description:
Learn piano, theory, and ear training through Uptown Funk — D Dorian, 7th chord inversions, voice leading & 4 funky comping patterns.

📥🎹 Download handwritten notes, staff notation & MIDI files + support us on Patreon 🎶✨ Get every variation from this Uptown Funk lesson 🔥
https://www.patreon.com/posts/uptown-funk-d-4-159448824

What if you could learn piano, music theory, ear training, AND arranging — all from one song? In this lesson, Jason Zac uses Uptown Funk by Mark Ronson ft. Bruno Mars as a vehicle for all four goals at once. The twist? There's no piano in the song.

We start by identifying the mode (D Dorian) and the two chords driving the whole track: D minor 7th and G dominant 7th. You'll learn minors in packs of four — Natural, Harmonic, Dorian and Melodic — so you'll instantly recognise the funky minor sound anywhere.

Then we get into the piano work: all four inversions of Dm7 and G7, voice leading through common tones, and rhythm patterns including block chords, octave toggling bass, staccato funk articulation, and triplet (tresio) feels. Every shape connects to a usable groove.

Next comes the song ingredient breakdown — vocal bass line on a 16th-note grid, Bruno Mars's vocal as the rhythmic engine, plus guitar comping, horn harmonies and the bass guitar. You'll learn to reverse-engineer a stereo file like a DAW, then translate those ingredients into FOUR funky right-hand piano patterns paired with a transcribed bass line.

Ready to practise smarter? Apply for our courses or browse the full video library at nathanielschool.com. Like, share, subscribe and hit the bell for more song-based piano lessons!
